Project Overview
text:
This project evaluates career opportunities for Data Scientists within the Software Publishers industry (NAICS 5132). The analysis is intentionally limited to this industry and career pathway so that the final product provides focused, decision-oriented guidance rather than a broad overview of the entire labor market.
Software publishers are a relevant setting for data science careers because software companies increasingly rely on large-scale data, machine learning, artificial intelligence, experimentation, and analytics to develop products and improve business decisions. The U.S. Census Bureau classifies Software Publishers under NAICS 5132, with the detailed 2022 industry code 513210 U.S. Census Bureau (2022).

title: Project Overview
text: What does the current job market look like for Data Scientists and closely related AI/ML roles within the Software Publishers industry, and which skills should students prioritize to improve their career readiness for these opportunities?

title: Project Overview
text: The primary user of this career evaluation product is a student or early-career professional interested in pursuing a Data Scientist career in the software industry. The product is designed to help that user understand job-market demand, salary and location patterns, common technical skills, and potential skill gaps.

title: Project Overview
text:
Data science remains a high-growth occupation as organizations continue to increase their use of data-driven decision making and artificial intelligence. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects substantially faster-than-average employment growth for Data Scientists and identifies the expanding use of AI and large-scale data as major drivers of demand U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2026).
The role also requires a broad combination of analytical, programming, modeling, and communication capabilities. O*NET describes Data Scientists as professionals who use programming, data mining, machine learning, natural language processing, modeling, and visualization to transform large datasets into useful information O*NET OnLine (2026). Because these requirements span multiple technical areas, students benefit from understanding which capabilities appear most frequently in real job postings rather than relying only on generic career descriptions.
Software publishing provides an especially relevant environment for this analysis because companies in this industry develop and distribute software products and are positioned to make extensive use of AI, machine learning, and data-intensive technologies U.S. Census Bureau (2022). Examining this industry therefore provides a focused way to evaluate the opportunities and skill expectations facing aspiring Data Scientists.

title: Project Overview
text:
Existing labor-market resources consistently emphasize both strong demand for Data Scientists and the multidisciplinary nature of the occupation. The Bureau of Labor Statistics identifies Data Scientists as a rapidly growing occupation and attributes this growth to increased demand for data analysis and AI-enabled business processes U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2026).
O*NET similarly characterizes the occupation around statistical analysis, programming, machine learning, data modeling, visualization, and interpretation of structured and unstructured data O*NET OnLine (2026). These occupational definitions provide a useful benchmark for evaluating whether the skills observed in Software Publisher job postings align with broader expectations for the profession.
Industry classification also matters because labor-market requirements can vary across sectors. The Census Bureau defines Software Publishers as organizations primarily engaged in producing and distributing computer software, including related design, documentation, installation, and support activities U.S. Census Bureau (2022). This makes Software Publishers an appropriate industry scope for evaluating technology-intensive Data Scientist opportunities.
Together, these sources support a career-evaluation approach that combines occupational benchmarks with real job-posting evidence. Our analysis therefore focuses on actual postings from the MET Career Compass dataset to evaluate demand, compensation, geography, work arrangement, and skill requirements specifically within Software Publishers.

title: Data Preparation
text:
The analytical dataset is restricted to the team’s selected industry and career pathway:

Industry: Software Publishers
NAICS: 5132
Career Pathway: Data Scientist

The MET Career Compass API was queried using NAICS 5132. The initial API pull returned 4,641 unique job postings.
To identify postings relevant to the Data Scientist pathway, job titles were normalized and searched for terms associated with Data Scientist and closely related AI/ML roles. These included:

Data Scientist
Machine Learning Scientist
Applied Scientist
Research Scientist
Machine Learning Engineer
ML Engineer
AI Engineer

This filtering approach was intentionally kept narrow so that the final dataset would remain aligned with the selected Data Scientist career pathway rather than expanding into unrelated analytical or software roles.



The project uses a staged Python pipeline:

01_pull_data.py retrieves Software Publishers job postings from the MET Career Compass API.
02_filter_data_scientist.py identifies Data Scientist and closely related AI/ML roles.
03_clean_data.py removes duplicate and staffing-agency records and creates cleaned analytical fields.
04_skill_summary.py summarizes selected technical skills.
05_data_dictionary.py creates a variable-description file.
06_market_summary.py produces baseline summary tables.

The API pull returned 4,641 unique postings. The career-pathway filter identified 8 relevant postings, including direct Data Scientist titles and related AI/ML roles. One staffing-agency posting was removed during cleaning, resulting in a final analytical dataset of 7 postings.



The API provides fields related to:

job title and normalized title;
company and organization;
posting date;
city, state, and geographic identifiers;
remote status;
employment type;
salary;
SOC and O*NET occupation classifications;
NAICS industry classification;
skills;
job description;
education and work-related signals.

The cleaned dataset retains the fields most directly related to the project’s market-baseline and skill-gap analyses.





Duplicate postings were removed using the unique job_id field.



Records identified as staffing-agency postings were excluded from the final analytical dataset so that employer-level findings would more closely reflect direct hiring organizations.



Salary fields were converted to numeric values, and nonpositive salary values were treated as missing rather than as valid compensation observations. A salary midpoint was calculated as the average of the reported minimum and maximum salary when both values were available.
In the enhanced dataset, usable salary midpoint information is available for 684 of 1,016 postings. Salary values vary substantially across postings, so both the median and distribution are examined in the Exploratory Data Analysis.



City and state fields were retained where available. Missing geographic values were classified as unknown rather than inferred. Geographic analysis focuses on reported state-level information to identify major employment markets.



Remote-work classifications were retained from the enhanced dataset. The final dataset contains 190 Remote, 31 Hybrid Remote, and 7 Not Remote postings. Another 788 postings have no identified remote classification.
Missing remote classifications are treated as unspecified rather than assumed to represent onsite positions.



Minimum and maximum years of experience were converted to numeric fields where available. Minimum experience information is available for 658 postings.
Missing experience requirements were preserved rather than estimated.



Education requirements were retained using the standardized education fields in the enhanced dataset. All 1,016 records contain an education classification, although 408 postings explicitly report “No Education Listed.”
This distinction allows postings without a stated education requirement to remain separate from postings that explicitly require a degree.



Standardized skill fields were retained for the Skill Gap Analysis. The dataset includes overall skills as well as specialized and software-specific skill classifications.
The skill lists were parsed into individual skills and counted across postings to measure employer demand. This allows frequently requested skills to be compared with the project team’s self-assessed proficiency.



Missing values were preserved and explicitly reported rather than replaced with estimated values. This is especially important for salary, experience, geography, and remote-work information.



Nonpositive salary values were treated as missing. Valid salary observations were retained even when unusually high or low because the postings span different employers, responsibilities, and seniority levels. The Exploratory Data Analysis therefore emphasizes the median in addition to the mean when interpreting compensation.
Original job titles were also preserved because the standardized Data Scientists occupational classification includes a broad range of titles.




The initial API pipeline produced a very small career-specific sample: 7 cleaned postings from 6 employers. While this process established a reproducible filtering and cleaning workflow, the sample was too limited to support meaningful comparisons of salary, geography, experience, education, and remote-work patterns.
For the enhanced Module 3 analysis, the project uses the larger job-posting dataset provided for the assignment. The same industry and career scope is maintained using:

NAICS 5132: Software Publishers
SOC occupation: Data Scientists

The industry and occupation filters initially identified 1,037 postings. After removing 21 staffing-agency postings and checking posting identifiers for duplicates, the final enhanced analytical dataset contains 1,016 postings from 174 employers.
The postings cover May 1 through September 30, 2024.
The enhanced dataset provides substantially better coverage for the variables required for market analysis:

684 postings contain usable salary midpoint information;
658 postings contain minimum experience requirements;
all 1,016 postings contain an education classification, including records explicitly classified as having no education listed;
remote-work classifications distinguish Remote, Hybrid Remote, Not Remote, and unspecified records;
city and state fields support geographic analysis; and
standardized skill fields support employer-demand and skill-gap analysis.

The enhanced dataset is therefore used as the primary analytical dataset for the Exploratory Data Analysis and Skill Gap Analysis, while the original API workflow documents the project’s initial data-acquisition and filtering process.



Although the enhanced dataset provides much stronger coverage than the original API sample, several limitations remain.
First, all 1,016 postings are classified as Data Scientists through the SOC field, but their raw job titles vary considerably. The sample includes analytics, artificial intelligence, consulting, implementation, business intelligence, and other related roles. Results therefore describe the broader occupational market represented by the Data Scientists classification rather than only jobs whose titles explicitly contain “Data Scientist.”
Second, the dataset covers only five months in 2024, so changes in posting volume should not be interpreted as long-term employment trends.
Third, salary and experience information are not available for every posting. Remote-work information is particularly incomplete because most postings do not contain an identified remote classification.
Finally, employer representation is uneven. Some organizations, particularly Oracle, contribute a large number of postings. Aggregate results may therefore reflect the hiring patterns of the largest employers in the sample.



The project generates and uses the following analytical outputs:

data/processed/data_scientist_software_publishers.csv — cleaned output from the initial API pipeline;
data/processed/data_dictionary.csv — variable descriptions from the initial pipeline;
data/processed/skill_summary.csv — initial technical-skill summary;
data/module3/data_scientist_software_publishers_clean.csv — enhanced 1,016-posting analytical dataset;
data/module3/top20_market_skills.csv — most frequently requested employer skills; and
data/module3/team_skill_market_demand.csv — employer demand for the technical skills used in the team comparison.

The large raw Module 3 dataset is kept out of version control. Analysis pages use the smaller filtered and processed outputs to reduce rendering time and avoid GitHub Pages issues.

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve()

load_dotenv(ROOT / ".env", override=True)

API_KEY = os.getenv("EMPLOYABILITY_API_KEY", "").strip()
BASE_URL = os.getenv("EMPLOYABILITY_API_BASE_URL", "").strip().rstrip("/")
PATH_PREFIX = os.getenv("EMPLOYABILITY_API_PATH_PREFIX", "").strip().strip("/")

if not API_KEY:
    raise RuntimeError("EMPLOYABILITY_API_KEY is missing from .env.")

if not BASE_URL or not PATH_PREFIX:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "EMPLOYABILITY_API_BASE_URL or "
        "EMPLOYABILITY_API_PATH_PREFIX is missing from .env."
    )

API_URL = f"{BASE_URL}/{PATH_PREFIX}"

HEADERS = {
    "X-API-Key": API_KEY,
    "Accept": "application/json",
}


import json
import time

RUN_TIME_SECONDS = 300
LIMIT = 100
SEARCH_QUERY = "data scientist"


data_scientist_json_file = (
    RAW_DIR / "data_scientist_query_naics5132_raw.json"
)

    RAW_DIR / "data_scientist_query_naics5132_raw.csv"

        saved_payload = json.load(file)

    all_rows = saved_payload.get("results", [])
else:
    all_rows = []

next_offset = len(all_rows)
start_time = time.monotonic()

while time.monotonic() - start_time < RUN_TIME_SECONDS:
    print(f"Requesting Data Scientist rows from offset {next_offset}...")

    response = requests.get(
        f"{API_URL}/jobs/",
        headers=HEADERS,
        params={
            "naics": "513210",
            "q": SEARCH_QUERY,
            "limit": LIMIT,
            "offset": next_offset,
        },
        timeout=180,
    )

    response.raise_for_status()

    page_payload = response.json()
    new_rows = page_payload.get("results", [])

    if not new_rows:
        print("No additional rows returned.")
        break

    all_rows.extend(new_rows)

    # Remove duplicate job IDs.
    unique_rows = []
    seen_job_ids = set()

    for row in all_rows:
        job_id = row.get("job_id")

        if job_id not in seen_job_ids:
            unique_rows.append(row)
            seen_job_ids.add(job_id)

    all_rows = unique_rows

    raw_payload = {
        "request": {
            "naics": "5132",
            "q": SEARCH_QUERY,
            "limit_per_page": LIMIT,
        },
        "results": all_rows,
    }

    with open(data_scientist_json_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        json.dump(raw_payload, file, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

    raw_df = pd.json_normalize(all_rows)
    raw_df.to_csv(data_scientist_csv_file, index=False)

    print(f"Saved {len(raw_df)} total Data Scientist query rows.")

    if not page_payload.get("meta", {}).get("next"):
        print("Reached the final page.")
        break

    next_offset += LIMIT

print("Finished the Data Scientist pull.")
print("Total saved rows:", len(all_rows))

Our Project Question
What does the current job market look like for Data Scientists within the Software Publishers industry, and which skills should students prioritize to improve their career readiness for these opportunities?

Career Pathway: Data Scientist
Industry: Software Publishers
NAICS Code: 5132
Primary Analysis Window: May–September 2024
Final Enhanced Dataset: 1,016 cleaned postings

title: Career Opportunities in Software Publishing
Career Opportunities in Software Publishing
text:
Key Market Findings
Our exploratory analysis identified several notable patterns:

Oracle is the largest employer represented in the dataset, with 392 postings.
California has the largest number of postings, followed by Illinois and Massachusetts.
Among postings with usable compensation data, the median annual salary midpoint is approximately $132,550.
Among postings reporting experience requirements, the median minimum requirement is 5 years.
A bachelor’s degree is the most common explicitly listed education level.
SQL, Python, and Tableau are among the most frequently observed technical skills included in our career-readiness comparison.
Communication and other professional skills also appear frequently, emphasizing that technical ability alone does not define career readiness.

The project progresses through four major analytical stages:

Project Framing — define the Data Scientist pathway and Software Publishers industry scope.
Data Preparation and EDA — collect, filter, clean, and analyze job-market data.
Skill Gap Analysis — compare employer skill demand with team proficiency.
Career Evaluation and Recommendations — translate the findings into practical career-development guidance.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
The Skill Gap Analysis compares the skills requested by employers in the Software Publishers job market with the current skill levels of the project team.
Employer demand is based on the 1,016 cleaned job postings used in the Exploratory Data Analysis. Team members separately rate their proficiency in selected technical skills on a 1–5 scale, where 1 represents no experience and 5 represents high proficiency.
This comparison helps identify:

the skills most frequently requested by employers;
the technical skills most relevant to Data Scientist career preparation;
areas where the team already demonstrates strength;
gaps between employer demand and current team proficiency; and
opportunities for future skill development.




The job-posting data contain both technical and professional skills. The following chart shows the 20 skills appearing most frequently across the 1,016 postings.

The cleaned dataset contains 1,016 postings from 174 employers between May and September 2024.
